name: Omar Fischer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent of AI firms, employers, unions, political parties and government; we don't sell or campaign. Your answers are confidential, including the parts you wouldn't say at work. What is a normal day like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead three audiobook-rights clerks inside a large publishing company. We check who signed for a recording, which edition it covers and what royalty the narrator or author receives. I moved from production scheduling into this junior lead post last year, and complex rights splits still send me to a senior colleague. I have a bachelor's degree and use an AI drafting tool now and then, but I check the contract myself.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What keeps you busy outside the office?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58 and live with Joan, who works shifts at a clinic. Our children are grown and have their own homes. We have a mortgage, my manager pay is high, and we have nine months of expenses saved; there are plenty of similar publishing offices nearby. Retirement is in sight, but we have not checked the two pensions' actual dates and amounts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small drafting helper can tidy a permissions email, but our authors still need the right payment and a real signature. I'm learning to lead three rights clerks, and the work is busy. My pay is high for this job, Joan's clinic wage is steady, and we have nine months of expenses saved, so the mortgage is comfortable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the clerks to attach an author's signed permission to every audiobook release. I'd tell the writers' association that we still review the royalty line, not just the summary. I use an AI drafting tool sometimes, but I wouldn't let it sign for an author.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I moved from production scheduling into rights last year and still ask a senior colleague to check complex royalty splits. In a plateau I expect the job to last, and there are plenty of similar publishing offices nearby. Nine months cash and two wages leave me room to learn without pretending I am already the best rights manager.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On Tuesday I'll review the eight audiobook releases missing a clear narrator consent line with the three clerks and request the signed pages. Through the first plateau year I'll keep using our existing draft helper only for wording after checking the contract. I'll add 220 monthly to cash if wages still cover mortgage, food and the clinic travel Joan needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm. A rights mistake still costs a person money, even when the software is modest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which consent line was missing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One narrator agreed to the original recording but not the new edition. The release list called the title cleared because an old file had a signature. An old signature is not permission for a new voice edition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your grown children need the reserve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own homes and jobs. We may help with a one-off problem if we can, but I don't count their bills as a standing part of ours. The nine months is primarily for our mortgage and health costs.

say: I'd tell clerks to attach **signed narrator consent** to new editions.
I'd tell the writers' association we check **royalty lines** ourselves.
think: I expect my new rights job to **last** in a plateau.
Nine months cash and two wages give me **room to learn**.
do: Review **eight audiobook releases** for narrator consent Tuesday.
Keep the **existing drafting helper** under contract review.
Save **220 monthly** only while wages cover mortgage, food and Joan's clinic travel.
feel: I feel **calm** about work and household money.
S0.quote: An old signature is not permission for a new voice edition.
fieldNote: A new audiobook edition lacked **fresh narrator consent** despite an old signature.
He uses AI **occasionally** and still checks complex royalty splits with a senior colleague.
Nine months cash and **high pay** make the plateau secure.

steps.text: Review eight audiobook releases for signed narrator consent Tuesday
Save 220 monthly only while wages cover mortgage, food and clinic travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing permissions, checking contracts, planning releases and answering authors fill my team's day. Stronger AI could do most of the first pass and leave fewer clerks. A person still records the book for now, but my manager work is nearly all documents and judgment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a paid test on old rights cases with a writers' representative present. I'd tell authors who is responsible for a mistaken permission and how to appeal. I'd ask the company to show the three clerks the staffing plan before a rollout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My junior lead post could be merged with a bigger audio team, even if the system keeps a human signer. I use AI sometimes, but that isn't the same as auditing every royalty calculation. Joan's wage and our nine months cash would let me compare offers rather than take the first title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In January I'd ask for a paid four-week closed-contract pilot, only if the rights director approves and the writers' representative has funded time. If the pilot catches the missing consent and both rights and finance leads approve its results, I'd learn the new audit view with a trained clerk on paid time. I'd use AI for routine permission drafts only after separate director rollout approval and human checks of every signature, and I'd apply to posted local rights jobs after checking pay and hours, leaving only for an affordable signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing a role I only recently learned. I have savings, but a good reserve does not turn a wrong release into a fair one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a bad release?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: An author could receive the wrong royalty because the model copied a split from an older edition. I want the signed page and the payment line next to each other. A smooth email cannot return a narrator's missing consent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would approve the pilot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rights director approves the paid test, and the rights and finance leads judge whether it worked. The director then decides whether it may touch new releases; those are separate decisions. A pilot isn't permission to publish a book.

I'd demand a **clear appeal route** for mistaken permissions.
think: My **junior lead role** could merge into a larger audio team.
Nine months cash lets me compare **real offers**, not assume my title survives.
do: Request a **paid closed-contract pilot** only with director approval and funded writer representation.
Learn the **audit view** after approved pilot on paid time; use routine AI drafts only after director rollout and signature checks.
Apply for **posted rights jobs** after pay and hours checks; leave only for affordable signed offer.
feel: I feel **anxious** about my post despite a strong reserve.
S1.quote: A pilot isn't permission to publish a book.
fieldNote: He wants authors to retain **human appeal** over royalty and consent errors.
Learning follows a **successful approved pilot**, while live rollout needs separate director consent.
A local job application does not mean he has **a signed offer**.

steps.text: Request paid closed-contract pilot only with director approval and funded writer participation
Learn rights audit view only after successful rights-finance test with paid trained-clerk instruction
Use AI permission drafts only after rights/finance pilot signoff, director rollout approval and human signature checks
Apply for posted rights jobs after pay and hours check; leave only for affordable signed offer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Full AGI by 2028 could check permissions, set royalty splits, draft letters and answer an author better and cheaper than our desk. AGI could synthesize a narrator's voice by 2028; setting up microphones remains physical until capable robots around 2031, but my role is not behind the equipment. Other local rights offices face the same thinking change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the clerks to ask for written notice and severance terms through the writers' association. I'd tell Joan we should postpone the planned boat holiday before the deposit. I'd tell authors they need a way to challenge a rights decision made by AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my rights lead post may disappear, though the firm might keep someone legally accountable. Our nine-month reserve and Joan's clinic wage would cover mortgage and food for a while, even if my higher pay stopped. I'd be unsettled about income in the years before a real pension, but I would not lose sleep tonight over next month's bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask the association representative to request written notice and redeployment terms and postpone the boat-holiday deposit. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my post ends, I'd apply for posted local paid work only after reading the actual duties and wage, accepting only a signed offer whose pay with Joan's confirmed income covers mortgage, food and clinic travel. I'd check pension eligibility and amount before considering retirement; if neither job nor pension covers our costs, I'd use the reserve to search and check public support eligibility before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about lost pay, but we have time to compare real numbers. I won't call a different rights desk safe just because its sign is familiar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a recording studio job last until 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A person might still move microphones until robots can do that around 2031, but I have no sound training or posted studio place. Booking and editing plans face AGI in 2028 anyway. I would not spend our reserve on a certificate without a paid opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your children to help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our children have families and bills of their own. Joan and I would discuss a one-off loan before asking whether either could afford it; we would agree repayment if one offered. I would not put their wages into our pension figures.

I'd tell authors to keep a **rights appeal** route.
think: My **rights lead post** may vanish, but an accountable human role could remain.
Nine months cash and Joan's wage would cover **essentials** without my pay.
do: Ask the **writers' association** for written notice and redeployment terms.
Postpone the **boat-holiday deposit** before paying it.
Apply for **posted work** after checking duties; accept signed offer only if combined Joan pay covers mortgage, food and clinic travel.
feel: I feel **anxious** about replacing high pay, without immediate bill fear.
S2.quote: I would not spend our reserve on a certificate without a paid opening.
fieldNote: He rejects an **untrained studio fallback** despite physical work lasting to 2031.
Other rights desks face **2028 AGI** too.
Pension and public support require **actual eligibility** before reliance.

steps.text: Ask writers association for written notice and redeployment terms
Postpone boat-holiday deposit before paying it
Apply locally; accept signed offer only if wage plus Joan's pay covers mortgage, food, clinic travel
Request pension eligibility and projected amount before considering retirement

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years might let me master the rights rules and build a larger buffer before AGI reaches our contracts in 2031. Recording equipment still needs hands until capable robots around 2034, but release schedules and royalty decisions change in 2031. I would not call a paid recording role mine because I can read a licence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company for a dated staffing plan and a worker seat at each review. I'd tell Joan we should compare pension statements with the mortgage before making travel plans. I'd tell authors how to challenge a royalty calculation as tools change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might stay employed until 2031, but my new manager title could still disappear. I don't know when our pensions can actually be drawn or what they pay, so I will not retire at sixty-three on an estimate. Nine months cash lets me negotiate a transition instead of walking away in anger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2027 I'd ask both pension providers for written eligibility dates and monthly estimates and compare the total with mortgage, food and clinic travel. I'd invest 180 monthly in a low-cost diversified fund only while nine months cash remains untouched and both wages pay essentials; I'd stop if Joan's hours fall. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, I'd apply for posted local work only where its wage with Joan's confirmed pay covers those bills, leaving my current job only for a signed offer or actual pension income that truly pays them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the desk, but five years gives me time to learn and check actual pension numbers. I would keep my emergency money out of the fund.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why invest instead of adding cash?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nine months in cash already covers a long search. The 180 is from wages after bills, and the fund can lose value; I would not treat it as a pension cheque. If the clinic cuts Joan's shifts, the contribution stops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you lead the whole rights department by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might learn enough, but I am a junior lead now and there are people who know far more about contracts. I would apply only if a real post opens and the pay is worth it. An older birthday does not give me a seniority badge.

I'd tell authors how to contest **royalty errors**.
think: My **junior manager title** could disappear in 2031, even if I stay employed until then.
I will not retire at sixty-three without **eligible pension income**.
do: Request **both pension statements** in 2027; stop work only if actual pension income covers household bills.
Invest **180 monthly** only after nine months cash and essentials, stopping if Joan's hours fall.
Apply for **paid work** only if wage plus Joan's confirmed pay covers mortgage, food and clinic travel; accept after signed offer.
feel: I feel **anxious** about work with time to check numbers.
S3.quote: An older birthday does not give me a seniority badge.
fieldNote: He may learn more rights law, but he is **still a junior lead**.
Fund contributions come from **paid wages** and stop if Joan's hours fall.
He distinguishes a **risky fund** from a pension payment.

steps.text: Request both pension dates and amounts; stop work only if actual pension covers bills

Apply locally; accept signed offer only if wage plus Joan's pay covers mortgage, food, clinic travel

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-eight in 2036, and our grown children will have their own bills. Rights decisions face AGI in 2036 and capable robots could handle physical recording equipment around 2039. I don't know whether our pensions would let both of us stop work then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the company and writers' association for annual reviews with a published staffing count. I'd tell Joan we should look at cash, mortgage and pension figures each year. I'd tell narrators to keep copies of consent for every new edition.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade could let us pay down the mortgage and learn whether the pension supports retirement, if both wages continue. My high pay and local alternatives give us choices, but they do not make a rights manager safe from AGI. I might stop at sixty-eight only after seeing eligible income that covers our bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I'd ask the writers' association to co-sign an annual staffing proposal, submit it only if they agree, and publish results only if the rights director approves. I'd put 350 monthly toward mortgage principal while nine months cash remains and both wages cover food and clinic travel, pausing if Joan's hours fall. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, I'd stop working only if actual pension income with Joan's confirmed pay covers mortgage, food and clinic travel; otherwise I'd apply for posted local work with manageable hours and an affordable wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the end of my desk, but the reserve and the time help. I need pension dates, not a birthday photograph.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children take over the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. They may visit and have their own families, and I would not write their incomes into our plan. The mortgage belongs to Joan and me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the pension is short?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would keep looking at paid posts rather than announce retirement. There are plenty of offices, though their rights work can change too. A job advert is not a wage until somebody hires me.

Pay **350 extra monthly** on mortgage only with nine months cash and both wages covering bills; pause if Joan's hours fall.
Apply for **posted local work** after 2036 if actual pension plus Joan's pay cannot cover mortgage, food and clinic travel.
feel: I feel **anxious** about my desk but able to plan.

Mortgage overpayments need **nine months cash** and Joan's hours maintained.
A signed job or real pension matters more than an **advertised title**.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the company would have little time to settle rights staff and author appeals before my desk changes. Written notice, a paid job with affordable wages, real pension figures and a human route for a narrator to contest a false permission would help. Nine months saved lets Joan and me ask for clear terms without claiming our current jobs are safe.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the narrator whose old signature was used for a new edition whether the release felt like consent. A file can be complete and permission still absent. I want a real person to answer when a voice is used without agreement.

headlineQuote: A file can be complete and permission still absent.
portrait: Omar, **58**, recently became junior lead of three audiobook-rights clerks after years scheduling production.
He has a bachelor's degree, uses AI **occasionally for drafts**, and still checks difficult rights splits with a senior colleague.
High pay, Joan's clinic wage and **nine months saved** support a mortgage while grown children live independently.
He seeks **writer representation** and real pension figures before leaving a paid rights role.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves little time for fair staff terms and author appeals before his desk changes.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **written notice** and a paid job whose wage covers household costs.
He needs **real pension figures** and a human route for narrators to contest false permissions.
